name: Tropical muted offbeat plucks
rationale: Short muted down-chops on every offbeat 'and', the classic tropical-house lilt sitting between the four-on-the-floor kicks. The quiet version plays only the 'and' of 2 and 4; the busy one plays all four offbeats and adds an up-stroke on the 'a' of 4. Bar 4 ends on a pushed chord at 3.5 ringing into the next phrase.

name: House offbeat stabs
rationale: Very short downward stabs on the offbeats, like an organ stab in a house track, leaving the downbeats to the kick. The quiet version stabs the 'and' of 1 and 3 only; the busy one stabs every offbeat plus a ghost up on the 'e' of 3. Bar 4 stops on beat 3 with one ringing chord.

name: Driving drop eighths
rationale: Straight down-up eighth notes for the drop, pushing the energy alongside the synths; the accent lands on the downbeats. The quiet version is downstrokes on each beat only. Bar 4 of the busy version breaks into sixteenths in beat 4 as a fill into the next phrase.

name: Half-time breakdown chords
rationale: Long ringing chords for breakdowns and builds: in the quiet version a chord on beat 1 and a second one pushed to the 'and' of 3, giving a half-time feel against the synth pads. The busy version adds a light up-strum on the 'and' of 2 and 4 between the ringing chords. Bar 4 holds a single whole-bar chord.

name: Syncopated 3.75 pushes
rationale: A pop-EDM push groove: chords on beat 1 and on the 'a' of 2, with the last strum of each bar pushed to 3.75 so it anticipates the next downbeat. The quiet version plays only the downbeat and the 3.75 push; the busy one adds the 2.75 push and a chop on the 'and' of 1. Bar 4 lets the push ring long into the next phrase.

name: Tropical sixteenth-note chops
rationale: Muted chops on the 'e' and the 'a' of the beat, giving the bouncy sixteenth feel of tropical house without cluttering the downbeats. The quiet version uses only the 'a' of 1 and 3; the busy one alternates 'e' downs and 'a' ups through the bar. Bar 4 drops out after beat 2 and leaves a single pushed chord on 3.75.

name: Future-bass upstroke swells
rationale: Long up-strums that ring like a future-bass chord swell, placed on the offbeat so they bloom between the kick hits. The quiet version has one long up-strum on the 'and' of 1 and another on the 'and' of 3; the busy version adds short down chops on 2 and 4 under them. Bar 4 ends with a long down chord from beat 2.

name: Progressive quarter pulse
rationale: A steady quarter-note pulse of short downstrokes with an accent pattern of 3+3+2 eighths over two bars, typical of a progressive-house build. The quiet version plays the dotted-quarter positions 0, 1.5 and 3; the busy version fills in the up-strokes between them. Bar 4 holds a long chord on 3 ringing into the next bar.

name: Dance-pop down-up chop
rationale: A pop-EDM strum of a long chord on beat 1 followed by a short down-up pair on 2.5 and 2.75, leaving beat 4 open for the vocal. The quiet version only rings the downbeat and one chop on 2.5; the busy one adds a chop on the 'and' of 3 and an up on the 'a' of 4. Bar 4 replaces the pair with a sixteenth fill on beat 4.

name: Tropical plucks with picked answers
rationale: Offbeat muted strums on the 'and' of 2 and 4 with a single picked high string answering on the 'a' of 3, giving a marimba-like tropical colour. The busy version adds offbeat chops on the 'and' of 1 and 3 too. Bar 4 picks a little rising three-note answer and ends on a ringing chord.

name: Build-up accelerating strums
rationale: A riser groove for builds: the number of strums grows through the phrase, as a snare roll would. The quiet version goes from one long chord per bar to two and four, then sixteenths in bar 4; the busy version starts at quarters and climbs to eighths and sixteenths. Bar 4 is the climax of the roll into the drop.

name: Shuffled house offbeats
rationale: A shuffled house groove written in eighth-note triplets: short chops on the last triplet of each beat, so they swing just behind the straight offbeat. The quiet version uses the swung offbeat of 2 and 4 only; the busy one adds the swung offbeat of 1 and 3 and an up on the middle triplet of 4. Bar 4 ends on a long chord on beat 3.

name: Stop-and-ring drop hits
rationale: Big ringing hits for a drop that leaves room for a lead synth: a long chord on 1 and a pushed one on the 'and' of 2. The quiet version rings the downbeat and adds one short chop on the 'a' of 3. The busy version adds an up-strum on the 'a' of 3 and a down on beat 4. Bar 4 stops dead after beat 2 with a scratch noise before the next phrase.

name: Offbeat up-stroke chops
rationale: The same tropical offbeat idea played with light up-strokes instead of downs, giving a softer, airier tick. The quiet version uses up-strokes on the 'and' of every beat but only in the high strings feel; the busy version adds down-strokes on the 'e' to make a sixteenth pair. Bar 4 lets the last up-stroke ring.

name: Deep-house sparse stab
rationale: A laid-back deep-house figure: a single stab on the 'a' of 1 and a ringing chord on the 'and' of 3, a two-bar call that leaves lots of air. The busy version adds a short chop on the 'and' of 2 and the 'a' of 4. Bar 4 plays one long chord from the 'and' of 1.

name: Tresillo pop-EDM drop
rationale: A 3-3-2 tresillo rhythm (beats 0, 0.75 and 1.5 repeated across the bar) as heard in many dance-pop drops, played as down chops. The quiet version plays the tresillo once per bar as 0, 1.5 and 3; the busy version uses the double-time tresillo 0, 0.75, 1.5, 2, 2.75, 3.5. Bar 4 turns the last group into a long ringing chord.

name: Bright acoustic pop-EDM strum
rationale: A bright acoustic strum in the classic down, down-up, up-down-up shape adapted for dance pop, with the upstrokes on the 'and' of 2, 3 and 4. The quiet version plays only beat 1, the 'and' of 2 and beat 4. Bar 4 ends with a long down on 3 and a slide noise into the next phrase.

name: Bass-pick and offbeat stab
rationale: A picked bass string on the downbeat answered by a short chord stab on the offbeat, a light 'boom-chick' that sits under a kick and lead synth. The quiet version picks on 1 and 3 with stabs on the 'and' of 2 and 4; the busy version stabs every offbeat. Bar 4 ends with a long chord on beat 3.

name: Anticipated chord pushes
rationale: Each bar's chord is struck early, on the 'and' of 4 of the bar before, and left to ring through the downbeat, which makes chord changes feel pulled forward. The quiet version has only that push plus a soft up on 2; the busy version adds chops on the 'and' of 1, 2 and 3. Bar 4 pushes on 3.75 instead, a sixteenth later and tighter.

name: Two-bar call and response
rationale: A two-bar phrase: bar one is a short chopped rhythm (the call) and bar two answers with long ringing chords. The quiet version calls with two chops and answers with one long chord; the busy version calls with a sixteenth figure and answers with two long chords and an up-strum. Bar 4 answers with a stop and a pushed chord.

name: Future-bass triplet rolls
rationale: Triplet strums imitating the rolled, wobbly chords of future bass: a long chord on 1, then a quick triplet down-up-down roll leading into beat 3. The quiet version plays only the long chord and one triplet pair into 3; the busy version rolls triplets into both beat 3 and the next downbeat. Bar 4 rings a whole-bar chord from beat 2.

name: Galloping sixteenth drop
rationale: A galloping figure (eighth plus two sixteenths: down on the beat, down-up on the 'and' and 'a') for a high-energy drop. The quiet version gallops only on beats 1 and 3; the busy one gallops on every beat. Bar 4 gallops through beat 2 then rings a long chord.

name: Breakdown picked arpeggio with chords
rationale: For quiet breakdowns: a ringing chord on beat 1 with a picked arpeggio climbing through the shape on the following eighths, with a soft long up-strum on the 'and' of 4. The busy version adds a soft up-strum on the 'and' of 2 and a second ringing chord on 3. Bar 4 picks the arpeggio back down and leaves a long chord on 3.

name: Off-sixteenth skank
rationale: A skipping offbeat skank with a down on the 'and' and an up on the 'a' of the same beat, like a reggae-tinged tropical house chop. The quiet version plays that pair on beats 2 and 4; the busy version on every beat. Bar 4 leaves out the last pair and lets the one on beat 3 ring.

name: Clean electric quarter chops
rationale: A clean electric guitar chopping short downstrokes on beats 2 and 4, doubling the clap, a nu-disco-flavoured house groove. The busy version adds sixteenth up ghost strokes just before each backbeat. Bar 4 replaces the beat-4 chop with a long chord pushed on the 'and' of 3.

name: Long up-strum shimmer
rationale: Soft, ringing up-strums placed on the 'and' of each half bar, a shimmering texture over pads in an intro or breakdown. The busy version adds a down-strum on beat 1 and a light up on the 'a' of 3. Bar 4 is one long up-strum from the 'and' of 1.

name: Sidechain-pump strums
rationale: Strums that imitate sidechain pumping: each chord starts on the offbeat and rings until the next kick, so the guitar swells and ducks with the kick. The quiet version rings on the 'and' of 1 and 3 with a short stroke on the 'and' of 4; the busy version swells on every offbeat with an up-tick on the 'e'. Bar 4 ends with a held chord.

name: Shuffled triplet dance strum
rationale: A swung dance-pop strum in triplets: down on the beat and up on the last triplet, giving a bouncy shuffle under a straight kick. The quiet version plays down on 1 and 3 with swung ups after them; the busy version plays the swung down-up on every beat. Bar 4 adds a triplet roll down-up-down into beat 4 and lets it ring.

name: Unison drop hits
rationale: Accented unison hits that lock with a synth riff in the drop: chords on 1, the 'a' of 1 and the 'and' of 3, with rests elsewhere. The quiet version keeps only the hits on 1 and the 'and' of 3; the busy version adds the 'a' of 1, beat 3 and a pickup up-strum on the 'a' of 4. Bar 4 plays four quarter-note hits as a turnaround.

name: Intro whole-bar rings with pickup
rationale: For intros and outros: one chord left to ring the whole bar, preceded by a quick up-strum pickup on the 'a' of 4. The busy version strikes on beats 1 and 3, each with a sixteenth pickup before it. Bar 4 rings from beat 1 with no pickup, closing the phrase.
